OpenAI no longer owns the majority of the AI market. For the first time, ChatGPT's share has dropped below 50%.

Sensor Tower's State of AI Report puts the numbers at: ChatGPT under 50%, Gemini at 27.7%, Claude at 10.3%. The remainder is fragmenting across open-source and specialized models — and that fragmentation accelerated this week.

Moonshot AI shipped Kimi K2.7 Code with 1 trillion parameters and OpenAI-compatible APIs. Z.ai released GLM-5.2 under MIT license with a million-token context window. Poolside shipped Laguna M.1 under Apache 2.0. These are not research previews. They are production-ready alternatives available today.

Meanwhile, Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro remains in preview as its availability timeline slips, and OpenAI teased GPT-5.6 — signaling that even the incumbents feel the pressure to announce faster than they ship.

For executives making AI platform decisions: the era of defaulting to one provider is over. The market is stratifying into tiers — proprietary frontier models, open-weight alternatives with zero licensing restrictions, and specialized vertical models. Your AI strategy needs to account for all three.

The companies that win will be the ones that treat AI model selection the way they treat cloud infrastructure — with redundancy, portability, and clear evaluation criteria baked into procurement.
